source.title: Investigating the Impact of Model Width and Density on Generalization in Presence of Label Noise
source.authors: Yihao Xue; Kyle Whitecross; Baharan Mirzasoleiman

record.tranche_reason: It sweeps model width and measures test loss, as in double-descent studies, and tests how label noise, sample size, regularization, and density affect the resulting curves.
record.gate_note: The paper reports width sweeps and test-loss outcomes under varied noise, regularization, sample size, and density. It also measures complexity proxies, but those are not test-error curves over epochs or a unified predictor of peak location. Values visible only in plots are recorded as figure only. Cited results from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps width under label noise and measures test loss in ReLU nets, ResNet34, ViT and random-feature ridge regression. This is the original model-wise recipe with noise and ℓ2 varied. It finds that sufficient noise adds a 'final ascent' after the second descent, which bears on V1, V4 and V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that a large enough noise-to-sample-size ratio adds a final ascent to the width curve, so the optimal width is intermediate. They attribute this to a change in the shape of the variance. They also find that stronger ℓ2 and robust methods make the ascent worse, that more data reduces it, and that lower density lets wider models generalize better under noise.
record.recipe_differences: Uses width sweeps and test loss as in double-descent work, but centers on noisy labels and adds density, sample-size, regularization, and robust-algorithm conditions; includes theoretical random-feature ridge regression and several classification settings.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported curve changes with label-noise level and type, ℓ2 regularization, sample size, width, density, and use of robust algorithms.

fits_no_version.finding: Under 40% noise, trajectory-length, bias-variance and spectral-norm complexity proxies rise with width; under clean labels they fall.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Label noise reverses the size–complexity relationship of learned functions.

fits_no_version.finding: Over density at fixed width, test loss decreases monotonically at low noise and becomes U-shaped at high noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under label noise, an intermediate density of trainable parameters is optimal.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI), 2022
record.problems: Most reported curve values are presented graphically without numerical estimates or uncertainty intervals in the text. Some sample-size comparisons report that final ascent is mitigated but do not isolate a fixed-width test-error increase near interpolation. The ELR comparison cited in the text changes noise and sample-size conditions, so it is not a matched comparison.
record.rows_left_out: Additional width, density, and robust-method results are shown in Figures 11–12 and 20–32, including several ELR and DivideMix conditions. They are not separately transcribed here because the main text already states the relevant curve patterns and the additional figure-only settings add substantial condition-by-condition detail. Appendix figures 21–28 also provide accuracy, bias, and variance plots not needed for the listed test-loss claims.

untested.parts: There is no test error over epochs.
There is no fixed-width test of more samples raising test error near interpolation. Larger samples are only shown to reduce the final ascent.
There is no single complexity measure that predicts peak location.
Neither triple or multiple descent nor optimally tuned regularization removing the peak is tested. The peak height itself is not measured.
Only random-feature regression and neural networks are studied; no other model classes.

missing.what: Final ascent in finite-n/d random-feature ridge regression for n/d = 0.5, 1, 2, 4, with p swept past n; plus the Table 1 variance shapes.
Variance shape changes from unimodal to increasing-decreasing-increasing as noise rises.
A final ascent under only 30% asymmetric noise on full CIFAR-10 with λ=5e-4.
ELR and DivideMix width sweeps on CIFAR-10/100 at various noise levels.

record.verdict_notes: Width is the size axis in every row; none of the experiments sweeps epochs or tests sample-wise non-monotonicity. Numbers are figure-only. R7's subject is mis-extracted.

versions.untested_parts: The tested settings focus on label-noisy training; the paper does not establish the curve across all deep-network settings.
It does not report test error over training epochs; appendix measures of parameter trajectory and variance are not epoch-wise test error.
Sample fractions are varied in width sweeps, but the paper does not report that increasing sample size raises test error near a fixed interpolation threshold.
The experiments do not test all model classes or establish a general curve specifically past an interpolation point.
It does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across width, epochs, and sample size.
It tests noise and regularization effects, but not multiple or triple descent, nor whether optimally tuned regularization eliminates the peak.
It does not re-count complexity using an effective parameter number to test whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shape.

rows.subject: 2-layer linear network with a random first layer
rows.size_stated: p hidden neurons; p/d varies
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical width sweep of random-feature ridge regression test risk under label noise.
rows.value: Risk has a minimum at an intermediate width; the variance can have an increasing-decreasing-increasing shape, producing a final ascent in risk.
rows.note: The result extends the usual fall-rise-fall curve with a further rise at sufficiently large noise-to-sample-size ratio.
rows.check: This is theory for a random-feature linear model, not a deep network, so V1 is dropped. With n/d=∞ the model never interpolates, so it cannot show behaviour past the interpolation point; the finite n/d results (Fig 5) are missing. For V6, noise produces a final ascent and the risk minimum sits at an intermediate width.

source_check.problem: An intermediate-width risk minimum in this noninterpolating limit does not establish a partial post-interpolation descent.
